questions.q: According to the chapter, architecture is the art and techniques of design and construction that combine which two aspects?
o: Functional and aesthetic aspects
Religious and political aspects
Natural and man-made aspects
Ancient and modern aspects
questions.a: Functional and aesthetic aspects: architecture combines how a structure works with how it looks.

questions.q:
Match each Harappan place or group in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Mohenjo-daro  2. Dholavira  3. Most Harappan cities  4. The 'Castle'
Column B: a. built with bricks, because they stood on alluvial plains where clay is abundant  b. the highest and most fortified area of Dholavira  c. wide streets and narrow lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions  d. extensive use of stone, because it was locally available
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: Mohenjo-daro had streets and lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions, Dholavira used locally available stone, most Harappan cities were of brick from the clay of the alluvial plains, and the Castle was Dholavira's highest and most fortified area.

questions.q: (a) Name any two features that, according to the chapter, characterise Harappan architecture. (b) Why were most Harappan cities built with bricks?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: carefully laid-out cities, standardised urban concepts, an emphasis on drainage, water management and civic organisation. (b) Most Harappan cities stood on alluvial plains, where clay (for bricks) is abundant.
s: (a) Names two features such as carefully laid-out cities, standardised urban concepts, or an emphasis on drainage, water management and civic organisation
(b) States that the cities were on alluvial plains where clay is abundant

questions.q: True or False? 'Almost every home in Mohenjo-daro had a bathing area, and the used water simply soaked into the ground beside each house.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Almost every home did have a bathing area, but the used water was taken out of the city through an efficient network of drains.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: used water was carried out of the city through an efficient network of drains

questions.q: A student argues that Dholavira kept the Harappan way of planning a city but changed the way of building it to suit its surroundings. Support the argument by giving (a) one feature that shows Dholavira followed Harappan planning, (b) the way in which Dholavira differed from most Harappan cities, and (c) why the surroundings explain that difference.
questions.a: (a) Dholavira is noted for its precise urban planning, with different fortified areas, streets and reservoirs, as Harappan cities were carefully laid out. (b) Unlike most Harappan cities, which were built of brick, Dholavira made extensive use of stone. (c) Stone was locally available in the Rann of Kachchh, while most other cities stood on alluvial plains where clay for bricks was abundant; each used the material at hand.
s: (a) Gives precise urban planning (fortified areas, streets, reservoirs) as the shared Harappan feature
(b) States that Dholavira used stone extensively while most Harappan cities used brick
(c) Explains that stone was locally available at Dholavira, while clay was abundant on the alluvial plains of the others

questions.q:
A museum in Bhuj is making a diorama that shows a corner of Mohenjo-daro beside the Castle entrance of Dholavira. Answer each question of the model-makers in one line, using the chapter.
(a) Which material should they use for the Mohenjo-daro houses?
(b) Which material should they use for the Dholavira gateway?
(c) How should the streets and lanes of Mohenjo-daro be laid out?
(d) What should run under the Mohenjo-daro streets to take used water away?
(e) What is the large room on the left of the Castle entrance, and what did the guards there do?
questions.a: (a) Brick. (b) Stone, in smooth blocks. (c) Wide streets and narrow lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions. (d) A network of drains that took used water out of the city. (e) A sentinel room, where guards screened people moving in or out.
s: (a) Brick for Mohenjo-daro
(b) Stone (smooth blocks) for Dholavira's gateway
(c) Wide streets and narrow lanes roughly oriented to the cardinal directions
(d) A network of drains carrying used water out of the city
(e) A sentinel room where guards screened people moving in or out

questions.q: A town builds two bus shelters. Shelter X has a strong roof and plenty of seats but looks dull and shapeless. Shelter Y has a graceful carved roof but leaks whenever it rains. Using the chapter's meaning of architecture, what does each shelter lack?
o: X lacks the aesthetic aspect and Y lacks the functional aspect
X lacks the functional aspect and Y lacks the aesthetic aspect
Both lack only the technical aspect, since neither is old
Neither counts as architecture, because neither is a monument
questions.a: X lacks the aesthetic aspect and Y lacks the functional aspect, since architecture combines both: X works but is not pleasing to look at, while Y is pleasing but does not do its job.

questions.q: Which of these is a stupa, as the chapter describes it?
o: A dome-shaped structure housing relics of the Buddha or revered monks
A pillared hall where monks gathered for assembly and for teaching
A cave carved into a hillside to serve as a dwelling for Jain monks
An ornamental gateway carved with many scenes of urban and village life
questions.a: A stupa is a dome-shaped structure housing relics of the Buddha or of revered monks.

questions.q: A carved panel from an early stupa shows people bowing before a pair of footprints and a wheel, with no human figure of the Buddha anywhere. Which explanation agrees with the chapter?
o: At this early stage the Buddha was shown symbolically, through objects, not in human form
The human figure of the Buddha was chipped away from the panel by later rulers
The panel shows Jain worship, so the Buddha could not appear in it at all
Early stupa panels showed only objects of daily life, never religious scenes
questions.a: At this early stage the Buddha was shown symbolically, through objects such as footprints, the wheel of dharma or the stupa itself, rather than in human form.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Ellora's cave no. 10, monks could walk all the way round the stupa.
Reason (R): The cave has an aisle, the corridor outside the row of pillars, in which monks would circumambulate the stupa.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the aisle outside the row of pillars is the corridor in which the monks walked round the stupa.

questions.q: (a) Why did rock-cut architecture develop among religious communities, according to the chapter? (b) Name the three purposes for which the caves were carved.
questions.a: (a) It was an efficient and durable mode of construction. (b) Worship, residence and assembly.
s: (a) States that it was an efficient and durable mode of construction
(b) Names worship, residence and assembly

questions.q:
Answer briefly about the main stupa at Sanchi.
(a) Who originally commissioned or patronised it?
(b) What is a torana, and what scenes do Sanchi's toranas depict?
(c) What is the vedika, and what did a worshipper do inside it?
questions.a: (a) Ashoka. (b) A torana is an ornamental gateway; Sanchi's depict many scenes of urban as well as village life. (c) The vedika is the enclosure of railings; inside it the worshipper circumambulated (walked around) the stupa.
s: (a) Names Ashoka
(b) Torana: ornamental gateway, showing scenes of urban and village life
(c) Vedika: the enclosure of railings, inside which the worshipper walked around the stupa

questions.q:
A school heritage club in Pune is preparing an exhibition on early Buddhist and Jain architecture and has three photographs.
Photo P: a hill near Bhubaneswar honeycombed with small caves; a board says the carving began in the 2nd century BCE under royal patronage.
Photo Q: a great dome in Madhya Pradesh surrounded by a ring of stone railings, with massive carved gateways.
Photo R: a vast dark hall in Maharashtra whose arched ceiling is ribbed like wooden beams; a seated figure in a teaching pose leans against a dome at the far end, behind a row of pillars.
(a) According to the chapter, who mostly lived in the caves in Photo P?
(b) Which of Q and R was built up from the ground and which was carved out of rock?
(c) What does the ceiling in Photo R imitate?
(d) The club has wall space for only two photographs. It wants to show both new ways of building that came with Buddhism and a custom of worship that the two places share. Which two photographs should it choose? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Jain monks; most of the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves served as their dwellings. (b) Q is a structural stupa, built up of stone like the main stupa at Sanchi; R, Ellora's cave no. 10, is rock-cut. (c) Beams of timber that existed in some urban buildings. (d) Q and R: Q shows structural stupa architecture and R shows rock-cut architecture, and at both worshippers circumambulated a stupa (inside the vedika at Sanchi, in the aisle at Ellora), the custom of pradakshina. P is also rock-cut, but its caves were dwellings and the chapter describes no stupa being walked around there.
s: (a) Jain monks (the caves were mostly their dwellings)
(b) Q built (structural stupa), R carved into rock
(c) Timber beams found in some urban buildings
(d) Chooses Q and R: one structural, one rock-cut, and both show circumambulation of a stupa; explains why P does not serve

questions.q: Compare the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves and the Ellora caves as rock-cut complexes, using the chapter. Write one point under each head: (a) where each complex is, (b) what the chapter says about when Udayagiri-Khandagiri was begun and what Ellora is renowned for, (c) which religious communities the caves of each served, (d) one fact that shows how much work the carving at Ellora involved.
questions.a: (a) Udayagiri-Khandagiri is near Bhubaneswar in Odisha; Ellora is in Maharashtra. (b) Carving at Udayagiri-Khandagiri began in the 2nd century BCE under royal patronage, among India's first; Ellora is renowned for its massive scale, exquisite craftsmanship and the technologies involved in the carving. (c) Most Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves were dwellings for Jain monks; Ellora has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves. (d) Many thousands of tonnes of rock had to be chipped away to leave the monolithic Kailasha Temple and the caves.
s: (a) Locates Udayagiri-Khandagiri near Bhubaneswar, Odisha, and Ellora in Maharashtra
(b) Udayagiri-Khandagiri begun in the 2nd century BCE (among India's first); Ellora renowned for scale, craftsmanship and technology
(c) Udayagiri-Khandagiri mostly Jain monks' dwellings; Ellora has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves
(d) Many thousands of tonnes of rock chipped away to leave the Kailasha Temple

questions.q: In which two states did a tradition of stepwells, called vavs or baoris, develop in classical times?
o: Gujarat and Rajasthan
Odisha and West Bengal
Uttar Pradesh and Bihar
Tamil Nadu and Kerala
questions.a: Gujarat and Rajasthan.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the water structures at Shringaverpur.
I. The reservoirs were fed by a channel from the Ganga during the river's seasonal flooding.
II. The last reservoir in the series was the one that allowed the silt in the water to settle down.
III. The Ramayana describes Shringaverapura as the place where Rama, Sita and Lakshmana crossed the Ganga at the start of their exile.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: it was the first reservoir or two that allowed the suspended silt to settle down.

questions.q: (a) What has India's monsoon-driven climate led people to develop for several millennia, according to the chapter? (b) Give the chapter's example of a simple water structure.
questions.a: (a) A great variety of structures for the harvesting, storage and distribution of water. (b) A humble village pond.
s: (a) Structures for harvesting, storing and distributing water
(b) A humble village pond

questions.q: True or False? 'The wells invented by the Harappans could not collapse inward under the pressure of underground water seeping in.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. They were built with trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together, so the wall could not be pushed inward.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the reason: trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together

questions.q:
A district survey lists three old water structures. X: a stone-lined tank attached to a temple, with stairways on all sides, used at festivals for rituals. Y: a well in Gujarat that goes down through several pillared levels decorated with statues. Z: a small mud-banked pond at the edge of a village.
(a) Give the chapter's name for the kind of structure X is and for the kind Y is.
(b) The survey team wants to leave Z out because it is 'too ordinary'. Using the chapter, explain why Z still belongs in a list of India's water structures.
(c) Give one use other than storing water that the chapter mentions for structures like X, and one for structures like Y.
questions.a: (a) X is a pushkarini (temple reservoir); Y is a stepwell (vav). (b) The chapter says the structures range from the simple, such as a humble village pond, to the highly sophisticated; all of them harvest and store water, so Z belongs. (c) X: water-based rituals (temple tanks were also works of art). Y: a social space where people could sit together, enjoy cooler temperatures and exchange news.
s: (a) Names X a pushkarini and Y a stepwell (vav or baori)
(b) Uses the chapter's range from the humble village pond to sophisticated works to keep Z
(c) X: water-based rituals; Y: a social space with cooler temperatures for sitting and exchanging news

questions.q: 'India's traditional water structures are works of engineering, works of art and social spaces, all at once.' Justify this statement using the chapter: give (a) one Harappan example of engineering skill and how it worked, (b) one example from Shringaverpur of engineering design, (c) one example of a water structure that is also a work of art, (d) one use of such structures as social or ritual spaces. Then (e) say why the chapter adds that 'much remains to be done', naming two threats.
questions.a: (a) Harappan wells were built with trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together, so they could not collapse inward under the pressure of underground infiltration (Dholavira also had large reservoirs). (b) At Shringaverpur a series of interconnected reservoirs was fed by a channel from the Ganga in flood, and the first reservoir or two let the silt settle. (c) The stepwell at Rani ki Vav has multiple pillared levels and hundreds of magnificent statues; many temple pushkarinis, with numerous stairways, were also works of art. (d) Stepwells offered a social space to sit together, enjoy cooler temperatures and exchange news; pushkarinis served water-based rituals. (e) Many such structures now suffer from depleted water sources, maintenance issues, pollution and waste dumping; environmentalists, locals and NGOs only sometimes join hands to preserve them.
s: (a) Harappan wells of locking trapezoid bricks that cannot collapse inward (or Dholavira's reservoirs)
(b) Shringaverpur's interconnected reservoirs fed from the Ganga, the first ones letting silt settle
(c) A work of art: Rani ki Vav's pillared levels and statues, or a pushkarini with many stairways
(d) A social or ritual use: stepwells as cool meeting places, or pushkarinis for water-based rituals
(e) Two threats (depleted sources, maintenance, pollution, waste dumping) and that protection efforts are only occasional

questions.q:
Meera visits a famous old structure in Gujarat with her family in May. A long flight of steps leads down through several pillared levels lined with hundreds of carved statues to the water at the bottom. The guide says: 'Long ago, families came down here on hot afternoons. Today the water level has dropped, plastic bottles float on the surface, and the trust has only three cleaners for the whole site.'
(a) What kind of water structure is this, and what is it called in the local language?
(b) Why would families have come down here on hot afternoons, according to the chapter?
(c) Name two threats the chapter lists that you can see in the guide's words.
(d) Name the groups who, the chapter says, sometimes join hands to preserve such structures.
questions.a: (a) A stepwell, called a vav (or baori). (b) It was a social space where people could sit together, enjoy cooler temperatures and exchange news. (c) Any two of: a depleted water source (the water level has dropped), pollution or waste dumping (plastic bottles), maintenance issues (only three cleaners). (d) Environmentalists, locals and NGOs.
s: (a) A stepwell, called a vav or baori
(b) A cool social space to sit together and exchange news
(c) Two threats matched to the guide's words: depleted water source, pollution or waste dumping, maintenance issues
(d) Environmentalists, locals and NGOs

questions.q: What is the garbhagriha of a temple?
o: The innermost chamber where the image (murti) of the deity is kept
The pillared hall where devotees gather before entering
The ceremonial entrance gateway of a south Indian temple
The enclosure wall that runs around the whole temple
questions.a: The garbhagriha is the innermost chamber where the image (murti) of the deity is kept.

questions.q:
Match each part of a temple in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Gopuram  2. Mandapa  3. Shikhara  4. Prakara
Column B: a. a pillared hall  b. an enclosure around the temple  c. the ceremonial entrance of a south Indian temple  d. the tower above the garbhagriha in a north Indian temple
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b: the gopuram is the ceremonial entrance in south India, a mandapa is a pillared hall, the shikhara is the tower over the garbhagriha in north Indian temples, and the prakara is the enclosure.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's vertical picture of a temple as Purusha, the top of the shikhara stands for the feet.
Reason (R): A temple is planned as a representation of the human body, that of Purusha or the cosmic being.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: the temple does represent the body of Purusha, but the top of the shikhara or vimana corresponds to the head and the platform on which the temple rests corresponds to the feet.

questions.q: (a) In which era did classical temples emerge? (b) Name the two sources of support that, according to the chapter, paid for building many temples.
questions.a: (a) The Gupta era. (b) Royal patronage (as inscriptions show) and endowments from various donors.
s: (a) The Gupta era
(b) Royal patronage and endowments from various donors

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) What is the tower above the garbhagriha called in north Indian temples?
(b) What is the same tower called in south Indian temples?
(c) What is the main alignment of a temple generally, and which way does the garbhagriha face?
questions.a: (a) Shikhara. (b) Vimana. (c) The main alignment is generally east-west, with the garbhagriha facing east.
s: (a) Shikhara
(b) Vimana
(c) East-west alignment, garbhagriha facing east

questions.q:
A family from Madurai visits a large classical temple in south India and walks from the street to the shrine. Using the temple plan in the chapter, name in order the four parts below and say in one line what each is.
(a) The first structure they pass through from the street.
(b) The hall they cross next.
(c) The chamber they finally reach.
(d) The tower they see rising above that chamber.
questions.a: (a) The gopuram, the ceremonial entrance of a south Indian temple. (b) A mandapa, a pillared hall. (c) The garbhagriha, the innermost chamber where the image (murti) of the deity is kept. (d) The vimana, the tower above the garbhagriha in south Indian temples.
s: (a) Gopuram: the ceremonial entrance
(b) Mandapa: a pillared hall
(c) Garbhagriha: the innermost chamber holding the murti
(d) Vimana: the tower above the garbhagriha in a south Indian temple

questions.q: A guide is describing a NORTH Indian classical temple. Which description uses the chapter's terms correctly for such a temple?
o: A torana entrance, mandapas, and a shikhara above the garbhagriha
A gopuram entrance, mandapas, and a vimana above the garbhagriha
A torana entrance, mandapas, and a vimana rising above the mandapa
A gopuram entrance, mandapas, and a shikhara rising above the mandapa
questions.a: A torana entrance, mandapas, and a shikhara above the garbhagriha: the chapter gives torana for some north Indian temples and shikhara for the north Indian tower, which stands above the garbhagriha (gopuram and vimana are the south Indian terms).

questions.q: Who built the Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur around 1010?
o: Rajaraja Chola I
Sultan Ahmed Shah I
The Solanki or Chaulukya dynasty
The Bundela Rajput kings
questions.a: Rajaraja Chola I built the Brihadishvara Temple around 1010.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the great temples of the 10th century onward.
I. From the 10th century onward, temples in different parts of India grew in scale and began incorporating multiple shrines, amenities and enclosures (prakaras).
II. The Lingaraja Temple at Bhubaneswar is built from locally available sandstone and laterite stone.
III. The Nandi at the Brihadishvara Temple is carved from a single stone and sits in a pavilion facing the main shrine.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I, II and III
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
questions.a: I, II and III: all three statements match the chapter's account of these temples.

questions.q: A traveller's notebook describes a temple: 'Its pyramid-shaped tower over the main shrine rises more than 60 metres, and a huge Nandi carved from one stone sits in a pavilion facing that shrine.' (a) Identify the temple and the town it stands in. (b) Using the chapter, explain whether the traveller should call its tower a shikhara or a vimana.
questions.a: (a) The Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. (b) A vimana: the chapter calls the tower above the garbhagriha a vimana in south Indian temples (shikhara is the north Indian term), and Thanjavur is in Tamil Nadu in the south.
s: (a) Identifies the Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur
(b) Vimana, because it is a south Indian temple and the chapter uses vimana for the south and shikhara for the north

questions.q: The chapter says the Bishnupur temples are 'of a very different style' from the Dilwara Temples. Show this by comparing the two under (a) material, (b) the centuries in which they were built, (c) what their carvings or panels show.
questions.a: (a) Dilwara: white marble from the nearby Aravalli hills; Bishnupur: brick structures with terracotta panels that were carved by hand and then fired in a kiln. (b) Dilwara: between the 11th and 13th centuries; Bishnupur: the 17th and 18th centuries. (c) Dilwara: Jain tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians and ornamental patterns covering every surface; Bishnupur: themes associated with Radha, Krishna or Rama, and scenes from everyday life.
s: (a) White marble from the Aravalli hills against brick with fired terracotta panels
(b) 11th-13th centuries against 17th-18th centuries
(c) Tirthankaras, deities, dancers, musicians and patterns against Radha, Krishna, Rama and everyday life

questions.q:
'Indian temples grew from modest buildings into vast complexes, and building them became a highly technical task.' Analyse this statement using the chapter.
(a) What were temples like until the 8th or 9th century?
(b) What changed from the 10th century onward? Give two changes.
(c) Give one piece of evidence of great scale from the Brihadishvara Temple and one from the Lingaraja Temple.
(d) Apart from a large manpower and accomplished sculptors, whom did such architecture require, and why?
(e) What have recent studies shown about the planning of these temples, and with which structures elsewhere in the world does the chapter compare this?
questions.a: (a) They were modest in size. (b) In different parts of India they grew in scale and began incorporating multiple shrines, amenities and enclosures (prakaras), culminating in vast complexes. (c) Brihadishvara: vast mandapas and a vimana over 60 metres high (or the massive monolithic Nandi); Lingaraja: three large mandapas used for different purposes. (d) Highly skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen, because the work involved elaborate construction techniques. (e) Their planning involved a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry; the same is true of Egypt's pyramids and temples, Athens' Parthenon and medieval Europe's gothic cathedrals.
s: (a) Modest in size until the 8th or 9th century
(b) Two changes: grew in scale; multiple shrines, amenities or prakaras; vast complexes
(c) Evidence: Brihadishvara's 60-metre vimana or vast mandapas, and Lingaraja's three large mandapas
(d) Highly skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen, for elaborate construction techniques
(e) Mathematics, especially advanced geometry; compared with Egypt's pyramids, the Parthenon or gothic cathedrals

questions.q:
A teacher in Dehradun gives her class four cards about shrines and asks them to identify each one.
Card 1: Dedicated to a form of Sarasvati; scholars from different parts of India and the world came here; it flourished between the 6th and 12th centuries CE and is now in ruins.
Card 2: Amid cedar forests in Manali; built in the 16th century CE; dedicated to the wife of Bhima.
Card 3: About 124 stone temples in the Almora district.
Card 4: Founded by the fourth Sikh Guru; the building of it and its sarovar was continued in 1588.
(a) Name the shrine on Card 1 and the script linked to its development.
(b) Name the group of temples on Card 3 and its state.
(c) Name the shrine on Card 4 and the Guru who continued its construction.
(d) The class must pick one card for a project titled 'Shrines as centres of learning'. Which card should it pick, and why is a site in ruins still worth studying?
questions.a: (a) Sharada Peetha, a key site in the development of the Sharada script. (b) The Jageshwar Group of Temples, Uttarakhand. (c) The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Punjab; Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru. (d) Card 1: Sharada Peetha was a renowned centre of learning that drew scholars from India and the world and earned Kashmir the name Sharada Desh; though in ruins, the chapter says it remains an important part of India's archaeological and cultural heritage. The other cards describe sites of worship, not of learning.
s: (a) Sharada Peetha; the Sharada script
(b) Jageshwar Group of Temples, Uttarakhand
(c) Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib); Guru Arjan Dev
(d) Picks Card 1, giving its role as a centre of learning and its value as archaeological and cultural heritage despite being in ruins

questions.q: Which statement about the building of classical temples matches the chapter?
o: Their planning involved a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry
They were held together mainly by cement mortar spread between the stones
They needed accomplished sculptors but no skilled architects or engineers
Only India built sacred structures whose planning needed such geometry
questions.a: Their planning involved a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry, as recent studies have shown.

questions.q: What is the mihrab in a mosque?
o: The niche in the wall that points to the direction of Mecca
The tower from which the muezzin makes the call to prayer
A latticed stone screen that lets in light and air
An overhanging balcony added in Rajasthani buildings
questions.a: The mihrab is the niche in the wall that points to the direction of Mecca.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Large mosques where the Friday prayers are held are often called 'Jama Masjid'.
Reason (R): The word 'jama' means 'mosque', while 'masjid' means 'prayer'.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: 'jama' means 'gathering' or 'assembly' and 'masjid' means 'mosque', which is why the large mosque where the community gathers for Friday prayers is called Jama Masjid.

questions.q: (a) Besides being places of prayer, name two other roles that mosques serve, according to the chapter. (b) What are minarets, and what are they used for?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: centres for religious education, community gatherings, venues for lectures and discussions. (b) Minarets are towers on either side of the domes, from where the muezzin makes his call to prayer.
s: (a) Two roles: religious education, community gatherings, lectures and discussions
(b) Towers beside the domes from which the muezzin calls people to prayer

questions.q: True or False? 'A corbelled arch is cut out of a single large curved block of stone.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Corbelled construction means stacking blocks as in a staircase pattern, not cutting one curved block.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: corbelled means built by stacking blocks in a staircase pattern

questions.q:
Answer briefly about the Jama Masjid in Delhi.
(a) Who built it, and in which century?
(b) What move of his came just before he built it?
(c) What is written on its walls and arches?
questions.a: (a) The Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan, in the mid-17th century. (b) He moved his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (now Old Delhi). (c) Calligraphy (decorative writing) of verses from the Qur'an.
s: (a) Shah Jahan, mid-17th century
(b) He had moved his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad
(c) Calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an

questions.q:
Two students disagree about the Jama Masjid in Ahmedabad. Kiran says: 'It is an example of Indo-Islamic architecture.' Sameer says: 'It was built by a Sultan for Islamic prayer, so it is purely Islamic architecture.' Evaluate the two views.
(a) Give the chapter's meaning of Indo-Islamic architecture.
(b) What does the chapter say about the building's elements as a whole?
(c) Give two features of the mosque that point to Indian craftsmanship.
(d) Why must Kiran be careful when she says who actually built it?
(e) Decide whose view the chapter supports, and say what part of Sameer's view is still correct.
questions.a: (a) Architecture that blends Islamic building traditions with Indian craftsmanship. (b) This yellow sandstone structure has a blend of Hindu and Islamic architectural elements; architecture in Gujarat took on regional flavours. (c) Any two: intricate stone jalis (latticed screens), pillars of the same style as in some temples but without decorations, detailed carvings. (d) The chapter says only that these features have led scholars to suggest that local Hindu and Jain artisans, masons and stone carvers helped build it; it is a suggestion, not a proof. (e) Kiran's view is supported: it is Indo-Islamic. Sameer is right that it was built by Sultan Ahmed Shah I in the 15th century as a mosque for prayer, but a mosque built for Islamic worship can still blend Indian craftsmanship.
s: (a) Indo-Islamic: Islamic building traditions blended with Indian craftsmanship
(b) States that it blends Hindu and Islamic elements (regional flavour of Gujarat)
(c) Two features: jalis, temple-style pillars without decoration, detailed carvings
(d) Notes that scholars only suggest local Hindu and Jain artisans helped
(e) Supports Kiran, while granting that Sultan Ahmed Shah I built it as a mosque

questions.q: In an old building in Rajasthan, a visitor notices ornate overhanging balconies and small pavilion domes on the roof. What does the chapter call these two local features?
o: Jharokhas and chhatris
Jalis and mihrabs
Minarets and domes
Toranas and gopurams
questions.a: Jharokhas (overhanging balconies) and chhatris (pavilion domes).

questions.q: Why, according to the chapter, were forts often built atop a hill?
o: To command a view of the plains below
To stay close to rain clouds for drinking water
Because building stone was found only on hilltops
To keep the royal palace far from the city's temples
questions.a: Forts were often built atop a hill so as to command a view of the plains below.

questions.q:
Match each fort or palace in Column A with the fact the chapter gives about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Mehrangarh Fort  2. Red Fort, Agra  3. Orchha Fort-Palace complex  4. Mysuru Palace
Column B: a. named after red sandstone mined at Dholpur, some 60 km away  b. built by the Bundela Rajput kings on the banks of the Betwa  c. massive blocks of locally sourced red sandstone, overlooking Jodhpur  d. the residence of the Wadiyar dynasty
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d: Mehrangarh is of locally sourced red sandstone above Jodhpur, the Agra fort's red sandstone came from Dholpur about 60 km away, Orchha was built by the Bundela Rajput kings on the Betwa, and the Mysuru Palace is the Wadiyars' residence.

questions.q: A family from Bengaluru can visit the Mysuru Palace either on a Tuesday afternoon or on a Sunday evening, and wants to see the building at its most spectacular. (a) Which visit should they choose, and why? (b) Name the architectural style of the palace and the dynasty whose residence it is.
questions.a: (a) The Sunday evening: the palace is illuminated by nearly 100,000 lights every Sunday evening (and during festivals). (b) Indo-Saracenic architecture; it is the residence of the Wadiyar dynasty.
s: (a) Chooses Sunday evening because of the nearly 100,000 lights
(b) Indo-Saracenic style; the Wadiyar dynasty

questions.q: The Red Fort at Agra was shaped and reshaped by several hands. Trace its story using the chapter: (a) what the fort was like before Akbar, and what he did with it; (b) what Shah Jahan changed in it, and what later happened to him there; (c) what happened to many of its buildings in the 19th century.
questions.a: (a) It was originally made of brick and had fallen to ruin; Akbar made his capital there and rebuilt it, with palaces and gardens, living quarters and halls for public and private audiences; the fort takes its name from the red sandstone mined at Dholpur. (b) Shah Jahan, fond of marble, replaced many sandstone buildings with marble ones, in particular the palaces, and had three mosques built; his son Aurangzeb imprisoned him until his death in one of those marble palaces. (c) Many of the buildings were destroyed by British troops of the East India Company.
s: (a) A ruined brick fort, rebuilt by Akbar as his capital with palaces, gardens and audience halls
(b) Shah Jahan replaced sandstone palaces with marble and was imprisoned there by Aurangzeb until his death
(c) Many buildings destroyed by East India Company troops in the 19th century

questions.q: A state tourism board is making a poster titled 'A fort is both a shield and a home' and can show only one of two places: the Mehrangarh Fort at Jodhpur or the Orchha Fort-Palace complex. Using the chapter, (a) state the two roles of forts that the title refers to, (b) give the evidence the chapter offers for each role at Mehrangarh, (c) give the evidence the chapter offers at Orchha, and (d) decide which place better fits the poster.
questions.a: (a) A fort protected a kingdom from invaders (the shield) and accommodated the residences of the ruling and military classes, sometimes a palace or a whole city (the home). (b) Mehrangarh is an imposing structure of massive red sandstone blocks overlooking Jodhpur (shield); its palace has areas for royalty, separate quarters for men and women, staff quarters, and stables and barracks (home). (c) Orchha has three main palaces with ornate chambers, carvings and courtyards, and chhatris on the riverbank (home), but the chapter describes no defensive features there. (d) Mehrangarh, because the chapter gives evidence for both roles there, while at Orchha it describes mainly the palace side.
s: (a) Protection of the kingdom and residence of the ruling and military classes
(b) Mehrangarh: massive red sandstone overlooking Jodhpur, plus royal quarters, staff quarters, stables and barracks
(c) Orchha: three palaces, chambers and courtyards, with no defensive detail given
(d) Decides Mehrangarh, because it shows both roles

questions.q: What have many parts of the Mehrangarh Fort been converted into today?
o: A museum of the fort's and Rajasthan's heritage
A hotel run for visitors from other countries
Barracks for a regiment of the modern army
Offices and record rooms of the state government
questions.a: Many parts of the fort have been converted into a museum to preserve and showcase the fort's and Rajasthan's cultural heritage.

questions.q: A landscape designer is asked to plan the garden around a new memorial in the style of the mausoleums described in the chapter. Which plan follows that style?
o: A garden divided into four sections, laid out symmetrically around the tomb
A garden of winding paths with trees planted wherever they grow best
A single open lawn on one side of the tomb, with a car park on the other
A garden in three unequal parts, one for each of three cultures
questions.a: A garden divided into four sections, laid out symmetrically around the tomb: the chapter says these monuments embedded strict concepts of symmetry that extended to the gardens, and the Taj Mahal's charbagh gardens are divided into four sections.

questions.q:
Read the statements about tombs and cenotaphs.
I. In the Islamic world, mausoleums were often built for prominent rulers, members of the royal household or some renowned mystics.
II. Humayun's Tomb was commissioned by Humayun's chief wife, Bega Begum, in 1558.
III. Cenotaphs mark the places where a king or a member of his family was buried.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: cenotaphs only marked the places where a king or his family member was cremated, not buried.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Jaswant Thada at Jodhpur is a cenotaph, not a tomb.
Reason (R): Mausoleums were also a political statement, standing as a testament to the greatness of the royalty or their dynasty.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the Jaswant Thada is not a tomb because the person remembered is not buried there (it served as a cremation ground); the political meaning of mausoleums does not explain this.

questions.q: True or False? 'In the Taj Mahal, the charbagh gardens and the large arched doorways are of Persian inspiration.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter calls the Taj Mahal a confluence of three cultures, and names the charbagh gardens (divided into four sections) and the large arched doorways as its Persian features.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the reason: the chapter lists charbagh gardens and large arched doorways as the Persian part of the Taj's three-culture blend

questions.q:
Compare Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal, using the chapter.
(a) Who had each one built, and for whom?
(b) Name two features that, according to the chapter, mausoleums like these share.
(c) Explain how the designers of Humayun's Tomb influenced later Mughal buildings such as the Taj Mahal.
questions.a: (a) Humayun's Tomb was commissioned by Humayun's chief wife, Bega Begum, in 1558; the Taj Mahal was built by Shah Jahan in the mid-17th century as a mausoleum for his queen Mumtaz Mahal's tomb. (b) Any two: strict symmetry extending to the gardens, arches, floral motifs, latticework, calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an. (c) Humayun's Tomb was designed by Persian architects whose Persian aesthetics became part of the Mughal architectural tradition; the Taj Mahal's charbagh gardens and large arched doorways are of Persian inspiration.
s: (a) Bega Begum for Humayun (1558); Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal (mid-17th century)
(b) Two shared features: symmetry with gardens, arches, floral motifs, latticework, Qur'anic calligraphy
(c) Persian architects of Humayun's Tomb brought Persian aesthetics into the Mughal tradition, seen in the Taj's Persian-inspired features

questions.q:
A class of 40 students from Lucknow goes on a two-day heritage trip. On day 1, in Delhi, they visit Monument X: an upper level with marble domes, arches and six-pointed stars, in a complex that also holds the tombs of several Mughals. On day 2, in Agra, they visit Monument Y: a white marble building whose colour seems to change from morning to evening, with coloured stones set into its walls in floral designs and a garden laid out in four parts. A board at Y says that in the 1970s its marble began to show a yellowish tinge.
(a) Name Monument X and the person who commissioned it.
(b) Name Monument Y and say whose tomb it was built for.
(c) What caused the yellowish tinge at Y, and what step was finally taken?
(d) For a wall chart the class writes: 'Both X and Y show Persian influence.' Is this supported for both? Give one piece of evidence for each.
questions.a: (a) Humayun's Tomb, commissioned by Humayun's chief wife, Bega Begum, in 1558. (b) The Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan for his queen Mumtaz Mahal's tomb. (c) Air pollution from local industries using coal and other fossil fuels; after an expert committee's recommendations and a PIL in the Supreme Court, a ban was imposed in the mid-1990s to prevent industrial pollution in the area. (d) Yes. X was designed by Persian architects who brought Persian aesthetics; at Y the charbagh gardens and the large arched doorways are of Persian inspiration.
s: (a) Humayun's Tomb; Bega Begum
(b) Taj Mahal; for Mumtaz Mahal's tomb
(c) Industrial pollution from coal and fossil fuels; the mid-1990s ban after the expert committee and the Supreme Court PIL
(d) Supported for both: Persian architects at X; Persian-inspired charbagh and arched doorways at Y

questions.q: Which architectural style flourished in India during the British Raj, from the mid-19th to the early 20th century, blending Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements?
o: Indo-Saracenic architecture
Indo-Islamic architecture
Gothic architecture
Shilpashastra architecture
questions.a: Indo-Saracenic architecture.

questions.q: A student compares two churches. Church A, in Mysuru, has pointed arches and large windows of stained glass. Church B, in Kerala, has a sloped tiled roof, oil lamps and a traditional wooden roof inside. Which conclusion fits the chapter?
o: A imitates a European style, while B incorporates local Kerala traditions
Both A and B imitate the European Gothic style of the colonial period
A follows local Kerala traditions, while B imitates a European style
Both A and B are examples of the Indo-Saracenic style of the Raj
questions.a: A imitates a European style (Gothic, whose key features are pointed arches and large stained-glass windows), while B incorporates local Kerala architectural traditions.

questions.q: (a) Who owned the Chettinadu houses of Tamil Nadu, and what did they trade, and with which region? (b) Using the chapter, explain why these houses can be called a meeting point of India and the wider world.
questions.a: (a) A community of merchants who traded in rice, spices and gems with Southeast Asia. (b) Materials were sourced from several parts of the world, such as teakwood from Burma and marble from Italy, while craftsmen from all over India worked on the frescoes and other artistic elements.
s: (a) A merchant community trading rice, spices and gems with Southeast Asia
(b) Materials from abroad (Burma teak, Italian marble) combined with the work of craftsmen from all over India

questions.q: Students in a small town find an old, little-known monument in a state of neglect. A shopkeeper tells them: 'That is the government's job, not ours.' (a) What does the chapter say about the government's responsibility and what will happen if only the government acts? (b) According to the chapter, what must citizens do to begin with?
questions.a: (a) Government bodies are theoretically responsible for conserving monuments, but in practice much will be lost unless citizens feel equally responsible. (b) To begin with, citizens must learn to appreciate and admire this labour of our ancestors.
s: (a) Government bodies are theoretically responsible, but much will be lost unless citizens feel equally responsible
(b) Citizens must first learn to appreciate and admire the labour of our ancestors

questions.q: The central courtyard, with rooms organised around it, appears again and again in the chapter. Show that it is a long-lasting and widespread design by giving one point from the chapter about each of: (a) Harappan houses, (b) the havelis of Shekhawati, (c) the Chettinadu houses of Tamil Nadu.
questions.a: (a) Some archaeologists have remarked that the design was already in use in some of the larger Harappan houses some 4,500 years ago. (b) Shekhawati havelis in Rajasthan, the homes of the nobility and rich merchant class, have a central courtyard with elaborate decorations including painted frescoes. (c) In the Chettinadu houses of Tamil Nadu the central courtyard served for rituals, community gatherings and sun-drying papads and chillies. Together these show the design lasting over thousands of years and across far-apart regions.
s: (a) Already in some larger Harappan houses some 4,500 years ago
(b) Shekhawati havelis of nobles and rich merchants built around a decorated central courtyard
(c) Chettinadu courtyards used for rituals, gatherings and sun-drying papads and chillies, showing the design across regions

questions.q:
'Preserving India's architectural heritage cannot be left to the government alone.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter.
(a) How big is the task of conservation, and what will a traveller notice at many lesser-known monuments?
(b) What does the chapter say about the government's role?
(c) What does the chapter ask of citizens?
(d) Which Fundamental Duty in the Constitution supports this, and what does it say?
(e) Give your judgement on the statement, with one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) India has thousands of monuments, many of them centuries old, and many lesser-known ones are in a state of neglect; preserving them is very challenging. (b) Government bodies are theoretically responsible for this huge task. (c) Citizens must feel equally responsible and, to begin with, learn to appreciate and admire this labour of our ancestors. (d) The duty 'to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture'. (e) The statement is right: the chapter says that in practice much will be lost unless citizens share the responsibility, and the Constitution itself makes preserving heritage a duty of every citizen.
s: (a) Thousands of centuries-old monuments; many lesser-known ones neglected
(b) Government bodies are theoretically responsible
(c) Citizens must feel equally responsible and learn to appreciate the ancestors' labour
(d) Quotes the duty to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
(e) Agrees, because much will be lost unless citizens share the duty
